title: How Sam Parr gets useful negative feedback: an anonymous two-question Google Form
summary: Sam argues negative feedback is more valuable and actionable than positive feedback, provided you separate your performance from your self-worth. He shares a simple three-step method: send an anonymous strengths/weaknesses form to 10 close contacts, then act on the most common weaknesses.

principles.text: Negative feedback is more valuable and actionable than positive feedback, so actively seek it out.
principles.quote: Negative feedback is far more valuable and actionable than positive feedback

principles.text: Decouple performance from self-esteem so critique is about what you did, not who you are.
principles.quote: De-couple the performance from the self-esteem.

principles.text: Ask 10 close friends and co-workers for 3 strengths and 3 weaknesses via an anonymous form.
principles.quote: Create a Google Form with two questions: What are my 3 biggest strengths and 3 biggest weaknesses.

principles.text: Ask for strengths too as a red herring; it gets people talking and speaking their mind.
principles.quote: I added the 3 strengths part as a red herring…it’s a great way to get people to start speaking their mind.

principles.text: Make the form anonymous and frame it as self-improvement to get honest, useful answers.
principles.quote: Tell them you’re working on yourself and want feedback because you appreciate their opinion. Make sure to tell them the form is anonymous.

principles.text: Focus on the most common weaknesses mentioned, and keep them visible so you act on them.
principles.quote: Take the three most common weaknesses mentioned, print them out, and tape them to your bedroom door.
